body.heading: The classic, perfected
paragraphs: One seeker counts — traditionally to a number agreed in advance, eyes honestly covered — while everyone else hides. Then: “Coming, ready or not!” The seeker hunts; the found join in or race for home base, depending on your local law. The game is ancient — a Greek writer described a version of it two thousand years ago.
What makes it great is the double thrill: the hider's exquisite stillness as footsteps pass, and the seeker's slow detective work. Few games give you so much drama for standing still in a cupboard.

body.heading: Sardines: hide and seek in reverse
paragraphs: In Sardines, only one person hides while everyone else seeks separately. When you find the hider, you do not announce it — you silently squeeze into the hiding place with them. One by one the seekers vanish, until the last player left wandering wonders where on earth everybody went.
The round ends in helpless laughter as the hiding place — a wardrobe, a bush, the space under a table — overflows. It is hide and seek where the prize for finding is joining the secret.

body.heading: Try it: three ways to vanish
paragraphs: Rotate through the classics in one session: standard hide and seek, Sardines, and a torch-lit evening round where the seeker carries the only light (outdoors, with adults supervising and boundaries agreed).
Keep a family record of legendary hiding places — the spot nobody found until the seeker gave up earns its finder a title. Every house has one. The trick is remembering whose turn it is to enjoy it.

takeaway: Hide and seek turns patience into theatre; Sardines turns it into comedy, one silently-squeezing seeker at a time.
